author: haiku
reason: B gives a newcomer an easier model to hold: three phases (Mirror, Switch, Finish), design decisions that each say why (such as why the outbox lives in the source database and app.jobs is not used), concrete SQL for the one guarded copy, and a single switch procedure S used for every change of source, while A is rigorous but denser, with a control row that moves between stores and separate pause, drain and abort sequences that take more effort to piece together.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to learn the system from: it describes how things work today, gives the main design goal (a Postgres failure never fails a user request), explains the parts that run all the time (write fence, control row, copy rules, outbox workers) apart from the rollout steps, and ends with a table of failures, while A is tighter but leaves more of the runtime picture to be pieced together from its design decisions and its reusable switch procedure.

author: sonnet
reason: Document B opens with the core idea: one SoT/follower mechanism (commit with an outbox row, a quick copy, then repair) that simply runs in reverse after the switch. It explains its key choices, such as fences over flags and the outbox over Redis, and groups the rollout into clear phases, whereas A puts a long list of terms first and spreads the same mechanism across more dense sections.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to follow: it first explains how `users` works today, lays out the plan as eight ordered steps, describes how the running system behaves separately from the rollout checklist, and adds tables for where state lives and how failures are handled. A explains its core mechanism more crisply, but it leaves out today's baseline and spreads its runtime behaviour across the checklist.

author: haiku
reason: A is longer, but it spells out how each piece works: where state lives, how CAS writes keep updates from overwriting each other, what each rollback step does and where it keeps its state, how resume charges due periods, and a table of failure cases. B is easier to read but leaves gaps, such as how the old engine actually charges due periods after a new_only rollback, and it contradicts itself on decommissioning (automatic at day 35 versus a separate approval).

author: haiku
reason: A defines its terms first, explains how to read the diagram, and describes each mode and each rollback path in short plain steps, so a newcomer can follow how the system works; B is more rigorous on concurrency and failure cases, but at about three times the length, with heavy CAS detail and 17 open questions, it is harder to absorb on first contact.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to follow: it states the two governing invariants first, names the gates, adds "who charges / who writes the ledger" columns to the mode table, lists the four reconciliation outcomes explicitly and explains charge safety in its own section, while A has rigorous mechanism detail packed into denser prose and edge labels.

author: sonnet
reason: I'd rather be handed B because it starts by explaining how billing works today, then lays out the mechanisms end to end: ledger entries marked charged or not charged, in-flight charges drained, reprocessing writing to the ledger, gates reset by an epoch tag, and time in mode taken from the flag's history. A is tidier but leaves gaps, such as where reprocessed invoices go and how reconciliation finds periods that were neither charged nor recorded.

author: haiku
reason: B is quicker to learn from: it opens with the four ways checkout can end, walks the flow in plain words, and has a failure table showing what happens to the cart, the money and the stock, plus a short list of the guarantees that make it safe; A covers more edge cases but is denser.

author: haiku
reason: B explains more of how the system actually works: each diagram edge says whether it is an HTTP call, a broker event or a webhook, each step names its trigger and endpoint, it shows how the customer learns the result while payment is pending, and it covers more failure cases (lost Place order response, charge timeout, failed release or claim, duplicate broker events), though A is easier to read at first.

author: sonnet
reason: A opens with a summary that gives the reasons behind the design (reserve before charging, events so a service that is down catches up later), defines delivery semantics precisely, and covers crash, redelivery and stuck-payment cases consistently; B is easier to start reading, but it leaves gaps a newcomer would trip on, such as the HTTP-request-answered-by-event mix, creating the order before the cart fetch, and no handling for a payment that never resolves.

author: sonnet
reason: A starts with a one-sentence summary, a guide to reading the diagram and plain definitions, and its flowchart has short boxes that are easy to follow; B covers more failure cases and explains its reasons, but its diagram boxes run to paragraph length and its denser notes make it harder for someone new to grasp the flow.

author: haiku
reason: Document A opens with a plain summary of the current system and the new one, then gives a separate end-to-end runtime flow from enqueue to reconciliation, a failure table and a runbook, so a newcomer can see how the system runs before reading the rollout; Document B mixes the runtime mechanics into its rollout steps, which makes the working system harder to piece together, even though its invariants and background numbers are useful.

author: haiku
reason: B opens with a plain overview of how the system works today and after the change, then walks one notification through the whole path (enqueue, publish, accept, send, report, record, reconcile) and adds a failure table, so a newcomer sees the running system before the rollout steps; A spreads the same mechanics across its invariants and rollout steps.

author: sonnet
reason: A starts by explaining today's system and why it duplicates emails, then traces the new path in order from start to finish and puts every failure in one table; B scatters the same mechanics across its rollout steps and repeats itself, even though its single-owner state diagram is a useful anchor.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier to learn the system from: it first explains how sending works today and why that causes problems, then follows one notification from start to finish through both sides, and puts every failure case in one table, while A spreads the runtime behaviour and failure handling across 13 rollout steps.
